Industry News: Personal Copilot: Train Your Own Coding Assistant

📅 27 Oct 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in the ever-evolving landscape of programming and software development, the quest for efficiency and productivity has led to remarkable innovations.
  • Industry observers note that however, while these pre-trained models can perform impressively across a range of tasks, there's an exciting possibility lying just beyond the horizon: the ability to tailor a code generation model to your specific needs.
  • In this blog post we show how we created HugCoder 🤗, a code LLM fine-tuned on the code contents from the public repositories of the huggingface GitHub organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in the ever-evolving landscape of programming and software development, the quest for efficiency and productivity has led to remarkable innovations. One such innovation is the emergence of code generation models such as Codex, StarCoder and Code Llama. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating human-like code snippets, thereby showing immense potential as coding assistants.

Industry observers note that however, while these pre-trained models can perform impressively across a range of tasks, there's an exciting possibility lying just beyond the horizon: the ability to tailor a code generation model to your specific needs. Think of personalized coding assistants which could be leveraged at an enterprise scale.

In this blog post we show how we created HugCoder 🤗, a code LLM fine-tuned on the code contents from the public repositories of the huggingface GitHub organization. We will discuss our data collection workflow, our training experiments, and some interesting results. This will enable you to create your own personal copilot based on your proprietary codebase. We will leave you with a couple of further extensions of this project for experimentation.

Our desired dataset is conceptually simple, we structured it like so:.

Sources indicate that scraping code contents from GitHub is straightforward with the Python GitHub API. However, depending on the number of repositories and the number of code files within a repository, one might easily run into API rate-limiting challenges.

To prevent such problems, we decided to clone all the public repositories locally and extract the contents from them instead of through the API. We used the multiprocessing module from Python to download all repos in parallel, as shown in this download script.

A repository can often contain non-code files such as images, presentations and other assets. We’re not interested in scraping them. We created a list of extensions to filter them out. To parse code files other than Jupyter Notebooks, we simply used the "utf-8" encoding. For notebooks, we only considered the code cells.

We also excluded all file paths that were not directly related to code. These include: .git, __pycache__, and xcodeproj.

Sources indicate that to keep the serialization of this content relatively memory-friendly, we used chunking and the feather format. Refer to this script for the full implementation.

The final dataset is available on the Hub, and it looks like this:.

Industry observers note that for this blog, we considered the top 10 Hugging Face public repositories, based on stargazers. They are the following:.

['transformers', 'pytorch-image-models', 'datasets', 'diffusers', 'peft', 'tokenizers', 'accelerate', 'text-generation-inference', 'chat-ui', 'deep-rl-class'].

Industry observers note that this is the code we used to generate this dataset, and this is the dataset in the Hub. Here is a snapshot of what it looks like:.

To reduce the project complexity, we didn’t consider deduplication of the dataset. If you are interested in applying deduplication techniques for a production application, this blog post is an excellent resource about the topic in the context of code LLMs.

Recent findings suggest that in this section, we show how to fine-tune the following models: bigcode/starcoder (15.5B params), bigcode/starcoderbase-1b (1B params), Deci/DeciCoder-1b (1B params). We'll use a single A100 40GB Colab Notebook using 🤗 PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) for all the experiments. Additionally, we'll show how to fully finetune the bigcode/starcoder (15.5B params) on a machine with 8 A100 80GB GPUs using 🤗 Accelerate's FSDP integration. The training objective is fill in the middle (FIM), wherein parts of a training sequence are moved to the end, and the reordered sequence is predicted auto-regressively.

Why PEFT? Full fine-tuning is expensive. Let’s have some numbers to put things in perspective:.

Minimum GPU memory required for full fine-tuning:.

Recent findings suggest that since the hardware requirements are huge, we'll be using parameter-efficient fine-tuning using QLoRA. Here are the minimal GPU memory requirements for fine-tuning StarCoder using QLoRA:.

trainable params: 110,428,160 || all params: 15,627,884,544 || trainable%: 0.7066097761926236.

In the above calculations, we didn't consider memory required for intermediate activation checkpointing which is considerably huge. We leverage Flash Attention V2 and Gradient Checkpointing to overcome this concern.

Please refer to the model-memory-usage to easily calculate how much vRAM is needed to train and perform major model inference on a model hosted on the 🤗 Hugging Face Hub.

According to recent reports, we will look at how to do full fine-tuning of bigcode/starcoder (15B params) on 8 A100 80GB GPUs using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) technique. For more information on FSDP, please refer to Fine-tuning Llama 2 70B using PyTorch FSDP and Accelerate Large Model Training using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel.

The command to launch training is given at run_fsdp.sh.

The total training time was 9 Hours. Taking the cost of $12.00 / hr based on lambdalabs for 8x A100 80GB GPUs, the total cost would be $108.

We will look at how to use QLoRA for fine-tuning bigcode/starcoder (15B params) on a single A100 40GB GPU using 🤗 PEFT. For more information on QLoRA and PEFT methods, please refer to Making LLMs even more accessible with bitsandbytes, 4-bit quantization and QLoRA and 🤗 PEFT: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Billion-Scale Models on Low-Resource Hardware.

It has been revealed that the command to launch training is given at run_peft.sh. The total training time was 12.5 Hours. Taking the cost of $1.10 / hr based on lambdalabs, the total cost would be $13.75. That's pretty good 🚀! In terms of cost, it's 7.8X lower than the cost for full fine-tuning.

The plot below indicates the eval loss, train loss and learning rate scheduler for QLoRA vs full fine-tuning. We observe that full fine-tuning leads to slightly lower loss and converges a bit faster compared to QLoRA. The learning rate for peft fine-tuning is 10X more than that of full fine-tuning.

To make sure that our QLoRA model doesn't lead to catastrophic forgetting, we run the Python Human Eval on it. Below are the results we got. Pass@1 measures the pass rate of completions considering just a single generated code candidate per problem. We can observe that the performance on humaneval-python is comparable between the base bigcode/starcoder (15B params) and the fine-tuned PEFT model smangrul/peft-lora-starcoder15B-v2-personal-copilot-A100-40GB-colab.

Recent findings suggest that let's now look at some qualitative samples. In our manual analysis, we noticed that the QLoRA led to slight overfitting and as such we down weigh it by creating upcoming weighted adapter with weight 0.8 via add_weighted_adapter utility of PEFT.

It has been revealed that we will look at 2 code infilling examples wherein the task of the model is to fill the part denoted by the placeholder. We will consider infilling completions from GitHub Copilot, the QLoRA fine-tuned model and the full fine-tuned model.

In the example above, the completion from GitHub Copilot is along the correct lines but doesn't help much. On the other hand, completions from QLoRA and full fine-tuned models are correctly infilling the entire function call with the necessary parameters. However, they are also adding a lot more noise afterwards. This could be controlled with a post-processing step to limit completions to closing brackets or new lines. Note that both QLoRA and full fine-tuned models produce results with similar quality.

Sources indicate that in the second example above, GitHub Copilot didn't give any completion. This can be due to the fact that 🤗 PEFT is a recent library and not yet part of Copilot's training data, which is exactly the type of problem we are trying to address. On the other hand, completions from QLoRA and full fine-tuned models are correctly infilling the entire function call with the necessary parameters. Again, note that both the QLoRA and the full fine-tuned models are giving generations of similar quality. Inference Code with various examples for full fine-tuned model and peft model are available at Full_Finetuned_StarCoder_Inference.ipynb and PEFT_StarCoder_Inference.ipynb, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that therefore, we can observe that the generations from both the variants are as per expectations. Awesome! 🚀.

Sources indicate that you can easily configure a custom code-completion LLM in VS Code using 🤗 llm-vscode VS Code Extension, together with hosting the model via 🤗 Inference EndPoints. We'll go through the required steps below. You can learn more details about deploying an endpoint in the inference endpoints documentation.

Below are the screenshots with the steps we followed to create our custom Inference Endpoint. We used our QLoRA model, exported as a full-sized merged model that can be easily loaded in transformers.

In a recent development, just follow the installation steps. In the settings, replace the endpoint in the field below, so it points to the HF Inference Endpoint you deployed.

So far, the models we trained were specifically trained as personal co-pilot for code completion tasks. They aren't trained to carry out conversations or for question answering. Octocoder and StarChat are great examples of such models. This section briefly describes how to achieve that.

According to recent reports, if you have dabbled with Stable Diffusion models and LoRAs for making your own Dreambooth models, you might be familiar with the concepts of combining different LoRAs with different weights, using a LoRA model with a different base model than the one on which it was trained. In text/code domain, this remains unexplored territory. We carry out experiments in this regard and have observed very promising findings. Are you ready? Let's go! 🚀.

In a recent development, PEFT presently supports 3 ways of combining LoRA models, linear, svd and cat. For more details, refer to tuners#peft.LoraModel.add_weighted_adapter.

Our notebook Dance_of_LoRAs.ipynb includes all the inference code and various LoRA loading combinations, like loading the chat assistant on top of starcoder instead of starcodeplus, which is the base model that we fine-tuned.

In a recent development, here, we will consider 2 abilities (chatting/QA and code-completion) on 2 data distributions (top 10 public hf codebase and generic codebase). That gives us 4 axes on which we'll carry out some qualitative evaluation analyses.

If we disable adapters, we observe that the task fails for both datasets, as the base model (starcoder) is only meant for code completion and not suitable for chatting/question-answering. Enabling copilot adapter performs similar to the disabled case because this LoRA was also specifically fine-tuned for code-completion.

Now, let's enable the assistant adapter.

Question Answering based on generic code.

Question Answering based on HF code.

We can observe that generic question regarding scrapy is being answered properly. However, it is failing for the HF code related question which wasn't part of its pretraining data.

Sources indicate that on disabling adapters, we observe that the code completion for the generic two-sum works as expected. However, the HF code completion fails with wrong params to LoraConfig, because the base model hasn't seen it in its pretraining data. Enabling assistant performs similar to the disabled case as it was trained on natural language conversations which didn't have any Hugging Face code repos.

Now, let's enable the copilot adapter.

We can observe that the copilot adapter gets it right in both cases. Therefore, it performs as expected for code-completions when working with HF specific codebase as well as generic codebases.

Sources indicate that now, as a user, I want to combine the ability of assistant as well as copilot. This will enable me to use it for code completion while coding in an IDE, and also have it as a chatbot to answer my questions regarding APIs, classes, methods, documentation. It should be able to provide answers to questions like How do I use x, Please write a code snippet for Y on my codebase.

PEFT allows you to do it via add_weighted_adapter. Let's create a fresh adapter code_buddy with equal weights to assistant and copilot adapters.

Now, let's see how code_buddy performs on the chatting/question_answering tasks.

Industry observers note that we can observe that code_buddy is performing much better than the assistant or copilot adapters alone! It is able to answer the write a code snippet request to show how to use a specific HF repo API. However, it is also hallucinating the wrong links/explanations, which remains an open challenge for LLMs.

Below is the performance of code_buddy on code completion tasks.

We can observe that code_buddy is performing on par with copilot, which was specifically finetuned for this task.

Sources indicate that we can also transfer the LoRA models to different base models. We will take the hot-off-the-press Octocoder model and apply on it the LoRA we trained above with starcoder base model. Please go through the following notebook PEFT_Personal_Code_CoPilot_Adapter_Transfer_Octocoder.ipynb for the entire code.

Performance on the Code Completion task.

Sources indicate that we can observe that octocoder is performing great. It is able to complete HF specific code snippets. It is also able to complete generic code snippets as seen in the notebook.

Performance on the Chatting/QA task.

As Octocoder is trained to answer questions and carry out conversations about coding, let's see if it can use our LoRA adapter to answer HF specific questions.

Yay! It correctly answers in detail how to create LoraConfig and related peft model along with correctly using the model name, dataset name as well as param values of LoraConfig. On disabling the adapter, it fails to correctly use the API of LoraConfig or to create a PEFT model, suggesting that it isn't part of the training data of Octocoder.

I know, after all this, you want to finetune starcoder on your codebase and use it locally on your consumer hardware such as Mac laptops with M1 GPUs, windows with RTX 4090/3090 GPUs ... Don't worry, we have got you covered.

According to recent reports, we will be using this super cool open source library mlc-llm 🔥. Specifically, we will be using this fork pacman100/mlc-llm which has changes to get it working with the Hugging Face Code Completion extension for VS Code. On my Mac latop with M1 Metal GPU, the 15B model was painfully slow. Hence, we will go small and train a PEFT LoRA version as well as a full finetuned version of bigcode/starcoderbase-1b. The training colab notebooks are linked below:.

The training loss, evaluation loss as well as learning rate schedules are plotted below:.

Now, we will look at detailed steps for locally hosting the merged model smangrul/starcoder1B-v2-personal-copilot-merged and using it with 🤗 llm-vscode VS Code Extension.

The demo at the start of this post is this 1B model running locally on my Mac laptop.

Sources indicate that in this blog plost, we saw how to finetune starcoder to create a personal co-pilot that knows about our code. We called it 🤗 HugCoder, as we trained it on Hugging Face code :) After looking at the data collection workflow, we compared training using QLoRA vs full fine-tuning. We also experimented by combining different LoRAs, which is still an unexplored technique in the text/code domain. For deployment, we examined remote inference using 🤗 Inference Endpoints, and also showed on-device execution of a smaller model with VS Code and MLC.

Please, let us know if you use these methods for your own codebase!

Scoliosis5K: Multimodal Gait Analysis via Clip-Conditioned RGB-Silhouette Fusion

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (213 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Color walking video records body boundary motion alongside clothing folds, surface appearance, and recording-environment cues. To examine what an explicit binary silhouette contributes to participant-level classification of scoliosis-related gait when a classifier already observes the paired color sequence, we construct Scoliosis5K, a multi-site collection of 4,998 corridor-walking sequences across 3,010 participant identifiers in which RGB person crops, binary silhouettes, and two-dimensional poses share each recording identifier and frame index. Our architecture uses each patch's pixel deviation from its clip mean to weight two low-rank query and value updates inside a pretrained RGB encoder, fusing the resulting video representation with a silhouette transformer sequence and regional kernel ridge scores extracted from one native-resolution RGB frame per window. Across 988 participants in five participant-disjoint cross-validation folds and three training seeds, the complete system reaches 83.77% accuracy and 79.91% macro-averaged F1, compared with 83.27% accuracy and 79.56% macro-F1 when the video RGB encoder remains frozen under identical inputs. Zeroing the silhouette vector at fixed weights shifts overall accuracy by only 0.10 percentage points while raising positive-category recall from 68.52% to 77.78% and lowering recall for both remaining categories. Macro-averaged AUROC is 0.950 across the cohort and 0.879 among participant pairs matched on acquisition site and recording-count group.

Breaking: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets.

Rethinking Full-Weight LoRA with Domain and Task Adapter Scaling for Question Answering over Portuguese Well Drilling Reports

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (214 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.26833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains remains challenging, particularly for technical documents such as Portuguese well drilling reports, where annotated data are scarce and domain adaptation may compromise instruction-following capabilities. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, its scaling after training remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the impact of LoRA adapter scaling on question answering over Portuguese drilling reports using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed either directly on instruction-tuned models or on their base counterparts, with subsequent adapter transfer, while task-specific adapters are trained on WellQuest, an open-source question-answering dataset derived from Portuguese drilling reports. The two adapters are also combined using complementary weights. Scaling factors ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 are evaluated across multiple training checkpoints using BERTScore. Results show that fractional scaling consistently improves DAPT performance over full-weight application, increasing F1 from 68.8\% to 71.9\% for Qwen2.5-7B and from 63.2\% to 68.5\% for Llama-3.1-8B. QA adapters perform best at high but fractional weights, while base-to-instruct transfer yields better results than direct DAPT on instruct-tuned models. Adapter merging provides a modest improvement for Llama-3.1-8B. Overall, these findings demonstrate that post-training adapter scaling can improve domain adaptation without additional data or training.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The increasing adoption of Machine Learning (ML) models in high-stakes applications has raised critical concerns regarding their robustness against adversarial attacks. While extensive research has focused on adversarial example generation in image and text domains, the study of such examples in tabular data remains comparatively limited, despite its widespread use in real-world systems. This work introduces AURORA, a modular, open-source tool for evaluating the robustness of ML models on tabular data classification. It integrates multiple adversarial perturbation methods and evaluation metrics within a unified framework to systematically assess model behavior under adversarial conditions. Central to AURORA is its evaluation report, which focuses on robustness analysis by quantifying performance degradation, comparing the impact of different perturbation strategies, and identifying model vulnerabilities across features and input regions. The report is complemented by visual artifacts that facilitate the interpretability of robustness patterns. Additionally, AURORA incorporates a distance adjustment mechanism that penalizes implausible adversarial samples based on feature-level constraints, ensuring that the robustness assessment remains grounded in realistic perturbations and is therefore more reliable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of our Enterprise Hub initiative, we recently released support for Storage Regions.

According to recent reports, regions let you decide where your org's models and datasets will be stored. This has two main benefits, which we'll briefly go over in this blog post:.

Presently we support the following regions:.

But first, let's see how to setup this feature in your organization's settings 🔥.

If your organization is not an Enterprise Hub org yet, you will see the following screen:.

Any repo (model or dataset) stored in a non-default location will display its Region directly as a tag. That way your organization's members can see at a glance where repos are located.

In many regulated industries, you may have a requirement to store your data in a specific area.

For companies in the EU, that means you can use the Hub to build ML in a GDPR compliant way: with datasets, models and inference endpoints all stored within EU data centers.

If you are an Enterprise Hub customer and have further questions about this, please get in touch!

Storing your models or your datasets closer to your team and infrastructure also means significantly improved performance, for both uploads and downloads.

This makes a massive difference considering model weights and dataset files are usually very large.

As an example, if you are located in Europe and store your repositories in the EU region, you can expect to see ~4-5x faster upload and download speeds vs. if they were stored in the US.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.26809v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods upgrade an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the fast-moving world of Natural Language Processing (NLP), we often find ourselves comparing different language models to see which one works best for specific tasks. This blog post is all about comparing three models: RoBERTa, Mistral-7b, and Llama-2-7b. We used them to tackle a common problem - classifying tweets about disasters. It is important to note that Mistral and Llama 2 are large models with 7 billion parameters. In contrast, RoBERTa-large (355M parameters) is a relatively smaller model used as a baseline for the comparison study.

In this blog, we used PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) technique: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models) for fine-tuning the pre-trained model on the sequence classification task. LoRa is designed to significantly reduce the number of trainable parameters while maintaining strong downstream task performance.

The main objective of this blog post is to implement LoRA fine-tuning for sequence classification tasks using three pre-trained models from Hugging Face: meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf, mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1, and roberta-large.

Note: For reproducing the reported results, please check the pinned versions in the wandb reports.

Recent findings suggest that roBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT Approach) is an advanced variant of the BERT model proposed by Meta AI research team. BERT is a transformer-based language model using self-attention mechanisms for contextual word representations and trained with a masked language model objective. Note that BERT is an encoder only model used for natural language understanding tasks (such as sequence classification and token classification).

Sources indicate that roBERTa is a popular model to fine-tune and appropriate as a baseline for our experiments. For more information, you can check the Hugging Face model card.

It has been revealed that llama 2 models, which stands for Large Language Model Meta AI, belong to the family of large language models (LLMs) introduced by Meta AI. The Llama 2 models vary in size, with parameter counts ranging from 7 billion to 65 billion.

Recent findings suggest that llama 2 is an auto-regressive language model, based on the transformer decoder architecture. To generate text, Llama 2 processes a sequence of words as input and iteratively predicts the next token using a sliding window. Llama 2 architecture is slightly different from models like GPT-3. For instance, Llama 2 employs the SwiGLU activation function rather than ReLU and opts for rotary positional embeddings in place of absolute learnable positional embeddings.

The recently released Llama 2 introduced architectural refinements to better leverage very long sequences by extending the context length to up to 4096 tokens, and using grouped-query attention (GQA) decoding.

According to recent reports, mistral 7B v0.1, with 7.3 billion parameters, is the first LLM introduced by Mistral AI. The main novel techniques used in Mistral 7B's architecture are:.

PEFT, Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning, is a collection of techniques (p-tuning, prefix-tuning, IA3, Adapters, and LoRa) designed to fine-tune large models using a much smaller set of training parameters while preserving the performance levels typically achieved through full fine-tuning.

In a recent development, loRA, Low-Rank Adaptation, is a PEFT method that shares similarities with Adapter layers. Its primary objective is to reduce the model's trainable parameters. LoRA's operation involves learning a low rank revision matrix while keeping the pre-trained weights frozen.

RoBERTa has a limitatiom of maximum sequence length of 512, so we set the MAX_LEN=512 for all models to ensure a fair comparison.

From the performance results, we can see that RoBERTa is outperforming Mistral 7B and Llama 2 by a large margin. This raises the question about whether we really need a complex and large LLM for tasks like short-sequence binary classification?

One learning we can draw from this study is that one should account for the specific project requirements, available resources, and performance needs to choose the LLMs model to use.

Also, for relatively simple prediction tasks with short sequences base models such as RoBERTa remain competitive.

Tech Report: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (258 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what presently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that prodigy is an annotation tool made by Explosion, a tech giant well known as the creators of spaCy.
  • To foster this customisability, Explosion has started releasing plugins.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first main feature is that this plugin allows you to train and re-use Hugging Face models on your annotated data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that prodigy is an annotation tool made by Explosion, a tech giant well known as the creators of spaCy. It's a fully scriptable product with a large community around it. The product has many features, including tight integration with spaCy and active learning capabilities. But the main feature of the product is that it is programmatically customizable with Python.

To foster this customisability, Explosion has started releasing plugins. These plugins integrate with third-party tools in an open way that encourages owners to work on bespoke annotation workflows. However, one customization specifically deserves to be celebrated explicitly. Last week, Explosion introduced Prodigy-HF, which offers code recipes that directly integrate with the Hugging Face stack. It's been a much-requested feature on the Prodigy support forum, so we're super excited to have it out there.

Recent findings suggest that the first main feature is that this plugin allows you to train and re-use Hugging Face models on your annotated data. That means if you've been annotating data in our interface for named entity recognition, you can directly fine-tune BERT models against it.

After installing the plugin you can call the hf.train.ner recipe from the command line to train a transformer model directly on your own data.

It has been revealed that this will fine-tune the distilbert-base-uncased model for the dataset you've stored in Prodigy and save it to disk. Similarly, this plugin also supports models for text classification via a very similar interface.

This offers a lot of flexibility because the tool directly integrates with the AutoTokenizer and AutoModel classes of Hugging Face transformers. Any transformer model on the hub can be fine-tuned on your own dataset with just a single command. These models will be serialised on disk, which means that you can upload them to the Hugging Face Hub, or re-use them to help you annotate data. This can save a lot of time, especially for NER tasks. To re-use a trained NER model you can use the hf.correct.ner recipe.

This will give you a similar interface as before, but now the model predictions will be shown in the interface as well.

The second feature, which is equally exciting, is that you can now also publish your annotated datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. This is great if you're interested in sharing datasets that others would like to use.

We're particularly fond of this upload feature because it encourages collaboration. People can annotate their own datasets independently of each other, but still benefit when they share the data with the wider community.

Recent findings suggest that we hope that this direct integration with the Hugging Face ecosystem enables many users to experiment more. The Hugging Face Hub offers many models for a wide array of tasks as well as a wide array of languages. We really hope that this integration makes it easier to get data annotated, even if you've got a more domain specific and experimental use-case.

More features for this library are on their way, and feel free to reach out on the Prodigy forum if you have more questions.

Industry observers note that we'd also like to thank the team over at Hugging Face for their feedback on this plugin, specifically @davanstrien, who suggested to add the upload feature. Thanks!

arXiv:2611.26752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.26745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.

Update (02/2024): Performance has improved even more! Check our updated benchmarks.

In a previous post on the Hugging Face blog, we introduced AWS Inferentia2, the second-generation AWS Inferentia accelerator, and explained how you could use optimum-neuron to promptly deploy Hugging Face models for standard text and vision tasks on AWS Inferencia 2 instances.

In a further step of integration with the AWS Neuron SDK, it is now possible to use 🤗 optimum-neuron to deploy LLM models for text generation on AWS Inferentia2.

And what better model could we choose for that demonstration than Llama 2, one of the most popular models on the Hugging Face hub.

It has been revealed that our recommendation is to use the Hugging Face Neuron Deep Learning AMI (DLAMI). The DLAMI comes with all required libraries pre-packaged for you, including the Optimum Neuron, Neuron Drivers, Transformers, Datasets, and Accelerate.

Alternatively, you can use the Hugging Face Neuron SDK DLC to deploy on Amazon SageMaker.

Note: stay tuned for an upcoming post dedicated to SageMaker deployment.

Finally, these components can also be installed manually on a fresh Inferentia2 instance following the optimum-neuron installation instructions.

As explained in the optimum-neuron documentation, models need to be compiled and exported to a serialized format before running them on Neuron devices.

Fortunately, 🤗 optimum-neuron offers a very simple API to export standard 🤗 transformers models to the Neuron format.

This deserves a little explanation:.

Depending on your choice of parameters and inferentia host, this may take from a few minutes to more than an hour.

Fortunately, you will need to do this only once because you can save your model and reload it later.

Even better, you can push it to the Hugging Face hub.

Once your model has been exported, you can generate text using the transformers library, as it has been described in detail in this previous post.

It has been revealed that note: when passing multiple input prompts to a model, the resulting token sequences must be padded to the left with an end-of-stream token. The tokenizers saved with the exported models are configured accordingly.

The following generation strategies are supported:.

Most logits pre-processing/filters (such as repetition penalty) are supported.

For those who like to keep it simple, there is an even simpler way to use an LLM model on AWS inferentia 2 using optimum-neuron pipelines.

It has been revealed that but how much efficient is text-generation on Inferentia2? Let's figure out!

We have uploaded on the hub pre-compiled versions of the LLama 2 7B and 13B models with different configurations:.

Note: all models are compiled with a maximum sequence length of 2048.

The llama2 7B "budget" model is meant to be deployed on inf2.xlarge instance that has only one neuron device, and enough cpu memory to load the model.

All other models are compiled to use the full extent of cores available on the inf2.48xlarge instance.

Note: please refer to the inferentia2 product page for details on the available instances.

We created two "latency" oriented configurations for the llama2 7B and llama2 13B models that can serve only one request at a time, but at full speed.

We also created two "throughput" oriented configurations to serve up to four requests in parallel.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the models, we generate tokens up to a total sequence length of 1024, starting from 256 input tokens (i.e. we generate 256, 512 and 768 tokens).

Note: the "budget" model numbers are reported but not included in the graphs for better readability.

The encoding time is the time required to process the input tokens and generate the first output token. It is a very important metric, as it corresponds to the latency directly perceived by the user when streaming generated tokens.

We test the encoding time for increasing context sizes, 256 input tokens corresponding roughly to a typical Q/A usage, while 768 is more typical of a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) use-case.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Encoding time is expressed in seconds.

We can see that all deployed models exhibit excellent response times, even for long contexts.

The end-to-end latency corresponds to the total time to reach a sequence length of 1024 tokens.

It therefore includes the encoding and generation time.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Latency is expressed in seconds.

All models deployed on the high-end instance exhibit a good latency, even those actually configured to optimize throughput.

The "budget" deployed model latency is significantly higher, but still ok.

Recent findings suggest that we adopt the same convention as other benchmarks to evaluate the throughput, by dividing the end-to-end latency by the sum of both input and output tokens. In other words, we divide the end-to-end latency by batch_size * sequence_length to obtain the number of generated tokens per second.

The "budget" model (Llama2 7B-B) is deployed on an inf2.xlarge instance while other models are deployed on an inf2.48xlarge instance.

Throughput is expressed in tokens/second.

Again, the models deployed on the high-end instance have a very good throughput, even those optimized for latency.

The "budget" model has a much lower throughput, but still ok for a streaming use-case, considering that an average reader reads around 5 words per-second.

We have illustrated how easy it is to deploy llama2 models from the Hugging Face hub on AWS Inferentia2 using 🤗 optimum-neuron.

The deployed models demonstrate very good performance in terms of encoding time, latency and throughput.

Interestingly, the deployed models latency is not too sensitive to the batch size, which opens the way for their deployment on inference endpoints serving multiple requests in parallel.

There is still plenty of room for improvement though:.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.26734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.

arXiv:2611.26702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.

  • We are delighted to announce a new method that can essentially make Stable Diffusion and SDXL faster, as if they had been distilled using the LCM process!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that latent Consistency Models (LCM) are a way to decrease the number of steps required to generate an image with Stable Diffusion (or SDXL) by distilling the original model into another version that requires fewer steps (4 to 8 instead of the original 25 to 50). Distillation is a type of training procedure that attempts to replicate the outputs from a source model using a newly introduced one. The distilled model may be designed to be smaller (that’s the case of DistilBERT or the recently-released Distil-Whisper) or, in this case, require fewer steps to run. It’s usually a lengthy and costly process that requires huge amounts of data, patience, and a few GPUs.

Well, that was the status quo before today!

We are delighted to announce a new method that can essentially make Stable Diffusion and SDXL faster, as if they had been distilled using the LCM process! How does it sound to run any SDXL model in about 1 second instead of 7 on a 3090, or 10x faster on Mac? Read on for details!

Recent findings suggest that so, what’s the trick? For latent consistency distillation, each model needs to be distilled separately. The core idea with LCM LoRA is to train just a small number of adapters, known as LoRA layers, instead of the full model. The resulting LoRAs can then be applied to any fine-tuned version of the model without having to distil them separately. If you are itching to see how this looks in practice, just jump to the next section to play with the inference code. If you want to train your own LoRAs, this is the process you’d use:.

For more details on the process, please download our paper.

According to recent reports, fast inference of Stable Diffusion and SDXL enables latest use-cases and workflows. To name a few:.

Industry observers note that to gauge the speed difference we are talking about, generating a single 1024x1024 image on an M1 Mac with SDXL (base) takes about a minute. Using the LCM LoRA, we get great results in just ~6s (4 steps). This is an order of magnitude faster, and not having to wait for results is a game-changer. Using a 4090, we get almost instant response (less than 1s). This unlocks the use of SDXL in applications where real-time events are a requirement.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. The present article introduces an intermediate structure, termed the critical thalweg, which encompasses all critical points and exhibits key geometric properties. Beyond providing a geometric proof of Baldi \& Hornik's results using simpler assumptions than the existing literature, this framework offers a global view of the loss landscape that can be easily visualized in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss continues to decrease to its global minimum.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.26656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study computation in which a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) uses AI systems, abstracted as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs), to solve Weighted Set Cover. A pilot study demonstrates that an LLM can outperform weighted greedy. HSOs differ in capabilities, response distributions, latencies, and token costs. We study how the PTM selects HSOs to obtain, by a deadline and with a required success probability, a full cover satisfying a prescribed weight threshold, and we analyze expected token cost. For queries requesting full covers, assuming independent call successes and uninformative failures, we characterize by linear programming the minimum expected token cost for every feasible success probability. An optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches. Among policies attaining maximum success probability, the expected cost reduction of two-batch selection relative to querying all oracles in one batch is nonnegative and submodular. We construct an FPTAS for near-optimal cost reduction under heterogeneous response-time bounds. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm for positive integral expected token costs. For partial-cover responses, the PTM combines returned sets across batches and turns. Once their union covers the universe, it verifies total weight directly or obtains a guarantee from LP-dual tests on retained partial covers. We give one-turn probability, token-cost, and hardness results and adaptive token-cost bounds under per-batch assumptions. A constructed instance shows that residual-guided querying can reduce expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of possible residual subproblems.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.26504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning requires agents to adapt when the task changes while reusing what they know about the environment. Successor features separate dynamics from task-specific reward, but their effectiveness depends on the choice of base features. Taking the identification of entorhinal grid cells with eigenvectors of the successor representation as a design principle, we build this basis from eigenvectors of the transition matrix of a fixed reference policy. With such a basis, the successor features at a state-action pair are a linear combination of the base features at that same pair, which is not true in general, and the coefficients are known in closed form: each successor feature is its base feature multiplied by $\theta_i = 1/(1-\gamma\lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ is its eigenvalue. The long-term return is thus predicted from the same features as the immediate reward, no successor-feature network or replay buffer is needed, and adapting to a fresh task reduces to a linear regression on the reward. The agent acts greedily on the action values of the reference policy, which is one step of policy improvement over it and suffices to reach a single goal. In a two-goal gridworld, with the uniform random walk as reference policy, whose eigenvectors are the low-frequency Laplacian eigenvectors, agents built this way maintain near-maximal return across every change of goal, whereas SimpleSF and DQN lose most of their return at each change.

Open LLM Leaderboard: DROP deep dive

📅 01 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, three fresh benchmarks were added to the Open LLM Leaderboard: Winogrande, GSM8k and DROP, using the original implementations reproduced in the EleutherAI Harness.
  • In a recent development, DROP (Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs) is an evaluation where models must extract relevant information from English-text paragraphs before executing discrete reasoning steps on them (for example, sorting or counting items to arrive at the correct answer, see the table below for examples).
  • In a recent development, we added it to the Open LLM Leaderboard three weeks ago, and observed that the f1-scores of pretrained models followed an unexpected trend: when we plotted DROP scores against the leaderboard original average (of ARC, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA and MMLU), which is a reasonable proxy for overall model performance, we expected DROP scores to be correlated with it (with better models having better performance).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, three fresh benchmarks were added to the Open LLM Leaderboard: Winogrande, GSM8k and DROP, using the original implementations reproduced in the EleutherAI Harness. A cursory look at the scores for DROP revealed something strange was going on, with the overwhelming majority of models scoring less than 10 out of 100 on their f1-score! We did a deep dive to understand what was going on, come with us to see what we found out!

In a recent development, DROP (Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs) is an evaluation where models must extract relevant information from English-text paragraphs before executing discrete reasoning steps on them (for example, sorting or counting items to arrive at the correct answer, see the table below for examples). The metrics used are custom f1 and exact match scores.

In a recent development, we added it to the Open LLM Leaderboard three weeks ago, and observed that the f1-scores of pretrained models followed an unexpected trend: when we plotted DROP scores against the leaderboard original average (of ARC, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA and MMLU), which is a reasonable proxy for overall model performance, we expected DROP scores to be correlated with it (with better models having better performance). However, this was only the case for a small number of models, and all the others had a very low DROP f1-score, below 10.

During our first deeper dive in these surprising behavior, we observed that the normalization step was possibly not working as intended: in some cases, this normalization ignored the correct numerical answers when they were directly followed by a whitespace character other than a space (a line return, for example). Let's look at an example, with the generation being 10\n\nPassage: The 2011 census recorded a population of 1,001,360, and the gold answer being 10.

Normalization happens in several steps, both for generation and gold:.

However, the overall score is not computed on the string, but on the bag of words (BOW) extracted from the string, here {'recorded', 'population', 'passage', 'census', '2011.0', '1001360.0', '10'}, which is compared with the BOW of the gold, also normalized in the above manner, {10.0}. As you can see, they don’t intersect, even though the model predicted the correct output!

In summary, if a number is followed by any kind of whitespace other than a simple space, it will not pass through the number normalization, hence never match the gold if it is also a number! This first issue was likely to mess up the scores quite a bit, but clearly it was not the only factor causing DROP scores to be so low. We decided to investigate a bit more.

Extending our investigations, our friends at Zeno joined us and undertook a much more thorough exploration of the results, looking at 5 models which were representative of the problems we noticed in DROP scores: falcon-180B and mistral-7B were underperforming compared to what we were expecting, Yi-34B and tigerbot-70B had a very good performance on DROP correlated with their average scores, and facebook/xglm-7.5B fell in the middle.

You can give analyzing the results a try in the Zeno project here if you want to!

The Zeno team found two even more concerning features:.

In a recent development, at this point, we believed that both failure cases were actually caused by the same root factor: using . as a stopword token (to end the generations):.

We hypothesized that both these problems could be fixed by using \n instead of . as an end of generation stop word.

Sources indicate that so we gave it a try! We investigated using \n as the end of generation token on the available results. We split the generated answer on the first \n it contained, if one was present, and recomputed the scores. Note that this is only an approximation of the correct result, as it won't fix answers that were cut too early on . (for example floating point answers) - but it also won’t give unfair advantage to any model, as all of them were affected by this problem. However it’s the best we could do without rerunning models (as we wanted to keep the community posted as soon as possible).

The results we got were the following - splitting on \n correlates really well with other scores and therefore with overall performance.

A quick calculation reveals that re-running the full evaluation of all models would be quite costly (the full update took 8 years of GPU time, and a lot of it was taken by DROP), we estimated how much it would cost to only re-run failing examples.

Industry observers note that in 10% of the cases, the gold answer is a floating number (for example 12.25) and model predictions start with the correct beginning (for our example, 12) but are cut off on a . - these predictions likely would have actually been correct if the generation was to continue. We would definitely need to re-run them! Our estimation does not count generated sentences that finish with a number which was possibly interrupted (40% of the other generations), nor any prediction messed up by its normalization.

According to recent reports, to get correct results, we would thus need to re-run more than 50% of the examples, a huge amount of GPU time! We need to be certain that the implementation we'll run is correct this time.

Recent findings suggest that after discussing it with the fantastic EleutherAI team (both on GitHub and internally), who guided us through the code and helped our investigations, it became very clear that the LM Eval Harness implementation follows the "official DROP" code very strictly: a newly introduced version of this benchmark’s evaluation thus needs to be developed! We have therefore taken the decision to remove DROP from the Open LLM Leaderboard until a new version arises.

Sources indicate that one take away of this investiguation is the value in having the many eyes of the community collaboratively investiguate a benchmark in order to detect errors that were previously missed. Here again the power of open-source, community and developping in the open-shines in that it allows to transparently investigate the root cause of an concern on a benchmark which has been out there for a couple of years.

We hope that interested members of the community will join forces with academics working on DROP evaluation to fix both its scoring and its normalization. We'd love it becomes usable again, as the dataset itself is really quite interesting and cool. We encourage you to provide feedback on how we should evaluate DROP on this issue.

Thanks to the many community members who pointed out problems on DROP scores, and many thanks to the EleutherAI Harness and Zeno teams for their great help on this issue.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27911v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth.

Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (169 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.

Goodbye cold boot - how we made LoRA Inference 300% faster

📅 05 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
